demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
Fatima is seventy-five years old, though she moves like someone much older. She lives with her husband, Amir, in a quiet suburb—a house they bought when their son, Kamran, was still a child. Now Kamran is gone, and the house feels like a museum of things she no longer knows how to touch. The front garden, where he used to kick a soccer ball against the wall, she walks around entirely. If the ball were still there—rotting under the hedge—she might burn the house down rather than look at it.

The death happened eight years ago, on a Tuesday afternoon in late spring. Fatima was presiding over a custody hearing. She remembers the precise clack of the clerk’s heels on the marble floor when the young woman walked in with a note. *Your son has been taken to the hospital.* No further explanation. She rose, excused herself with the calm of any emergency, and walked out. By the time she reached the hospital, Kamran was dead. A sudden arrhythmia—no warning, no history. He was thirty-five, a professor of literature, healthy as anyone. The doctor used words like *unexpected* and *massive*. Fatima heard nothing.

In the months that followed, she returned to the bench. It seemed unthinkable not to. She had spent forty years in the courtroom—first as a public defender, then a prosecutor, then a district court judge. The robe and the gavel were her armor. But the armor had cracks. During a sentencing hearing for a young man convicted of vehicular manslaughter, she found herself unable to look at the defendant’s mother. The woman was wearing a gray hijab, just like Fatima had worn to Kamran’s funeral. Fatima’s throat closed. She slammed her gavel and adjourned early, leaving the courtroom without explanation. She never did finish that sentencing—a colleague had to take over.

She took early retirement six months later. Everyone called it a “dignified decision.” Fatima knew it was flight.

Now, at home, the symptoms are a quiet landscape of dread. She avoids the garden. She avoids the hallway where Kamran’s university graduation photo hangs—Amir took it down, but she notices the lighter rectangle on the wallpaper every time she passes. She avoids phone calls from friends who might say his name. Last month, a neighbor’s grandson rang the doorbell selling cookies for a school fundraiser. The boy was about Kamran’s build, same dark curls. Fatima stood frozen behind the door, hand on the lock, heart slamming, until the boy walked away.

She does not sleep through the night. Usually it is three o’clock in the morning, the same hour the hospital called. She wakes gasping, drenched, convinced she can still hear the ringtone. Her husband, Amir, stirs and reaches for her hand. She lets him hold it for a minute, then pulls away. She does not want him to see her cry again. She feels guilty for the tears—they make Amir sad, and he has been so patient. But she also feels a strange anger at his patience, as if his calm presence somehow diminishes Kamran’s absence.

The PCL-5 score of 38 reflects what she describes to her therapist in clipped, careful sentences: the intrusive images that come without warning—Kamran as a toddler, Kamran in his graduation gown, Kamran on the cold hospital bed. The nightmares. The way she startles when the phone rings or when a door slams. The sense that she is living behind glass, watching the world move while she stays still.

She recalls the day of the funeral with surgical precision. The imam’s voice. The weight of the earth on the shovel. The moment she looked at Amir and thought, *We are now the family that lost a child.* She has not set foot in a mosque since. On the rare occasion she sees a funeral procession, she turns the car around.

This morning, Fatima stands at the kitchen window, watching a single bird hop along the fence where Kamran used to sit and read. She does not open the window. She does not call Amir. She simply watches until the bird flies away, and then she turns back to the empty cup of tea, cold now, and waits for the next wave. It will come. It always does.
